titleEn: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble
progression: | Em Em | C D | Em Am | B7 Em |
intro: Nine verses, said on Friday evening as the fifth of the six psalms that open Kabbalat Shabbat, and the last of the group of enthronement psalms that runs from 93 through here. It is built around a refrain that says holy three times, at the end of verse 3, the end of verse 5 and inside verse 9, and those three points cut the psalm into three sections of decreasing distance: the peoples, then the footstool, then three men with names. For a learner it is a compact drill in the plural, singular and possessive of one noun: a people, the peoples, all the peoples, and then the same consonants again as a verb meaning He answered them.

stichs.en: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble.
He sits enthroned on the cherubim; let the earth shake.

verses.summary: Two statements of fact, each followed by an ordered reaction. The kingship is not argued for anywhere in the psalm; it is announced and the world is told to respond.

stichs.en: The LORD is great in Zion,
and He is exalted above all the peoples.

verses.summary: A location and a rank in one line. Greatness is placed somewhere specific, which is what separates this psalm from a general claim about divine power.

stichs.en: Let them praise Your name, great and awesome.
Holy is He.

verses.summary: The address turns to the second person for the first time, and the verse ends on the two words that will come back twice more. The refrain is the shortest sentence in the psalm.

stichs.en: And the strength of a king who loves justice:
You have established fairness,
justice and righteousness in Jacob You have done.

verses.summary: The hardest sentence in the psalm to construe, and also the point where power is given a content. Strength is not the ability to do anything but the preference for one thing, justice.

stichs.en: Exalt the LORD our God and bow down at the footstool of His feet.
Holy is He.

verses.summary: Two opposite motions in one command: raise Him, lower yourself. The place named is the lowest part of the throne, which is as close as the psalm lets anyone approach.

stichs.en: Moses and Aaron among His priests,
and Samuel among those who call on His name,
they were calling to the LORD,
and He would answer them.

verses.summary: The psalm drops from cosmic scale to three names, all of them intercessors rather than kings. The answer is put in a form that means it happened repeatedly, not once.

stichs.en: In a pillar of cloud He would speak to them;
they kept His testimonies and the statute He gave them.

verses.summary: The exchange is described as two-way and habitual. He spoke and they kept, in that order, so obedience is the answer to speech rather than the price of it.

stichs.en: LORD our God, You answered them.
A God who lifts away, You were for them,
and one who takes account of their deeds.

verses.summary: The one verse in the psalm that holds two incompatible things together and does not resolve them. Forgiveness and reckoning are stated of the same subject in the same breath.

stichs.en: Exalt the LORD our God and bow down at His holy mountain,
for the LORD our God is holy.

verses.summary: Verse 5 repeated with two changes: the footstool becomes the mountain, and the refrain stops saying He and says the name instead. The distance has closed and the psalm ends.

pardes.body: Three sections marked by three closing refrains. Verses 1 to 3 are the widest shot, kingship announced to the peoples and the earth. Verses 4 and 5 narrow to what the kingship consists of, justice established in Jacob, and to a place, the footstool. Verses 6 to 9 narrow again to three named men who spoke and were answered. Watch the pronoun in the refrain: {{3.4}} and {{5.6}} both say holy is He, and {{9.7}} says the LORD our God is holy, so the third repetition drops the pronoun and names Him. Watch the location too. Verse 5 sends the worshipper to the footstool and verse 9 to the mountain, which is the same instruction given twice with the second one closer in.

Verse 4 is the standing crux of the psalm. Its first words, {{4.0}} and {{4.1}}, sit in the sentence without an obvious verb, and the readings divide: some take the strength of the king as a continuation of the praise in verse 3, some read it as a fresh subject with the loving of justice as its predicate, and some translations insert a break and start over at You have established. The dispute is real and the Hebrew supports more than one solution. In verse 8, {{8.5}} is a participle from the root meaning to lift or carry, used elsewhere of carrying away guilt, while {{8.8}} is the participle for taking vengeance, and it is contested whether their deeds means the wrongs the fathers committed or the wrongs done to them. Note also {{7.8}}, a poetic form of the ordinary word for to them, which appears mostly in older verse and marks the register of the line.

Verse 6 calls Moses one of His priests, which is a problem the Torah does not obviously allow, since the priesthood is given to Aaron and his sons. The traditional answer is that Moses served as priest during the seven days of the Tabernacle's consecration, before the office passed to Aaron's line, so the verse is exact rather than loose. The grouping is itself an argument. Moses, Aaron and Samuel are three men remembered chiefly for standing between God and a people about to be punished, and they are produced immediately after verse 5 has put everyone on the ground at the footstool. The psalm answers the question a reader would ask at that point, which is whether anything said from that position is ever heard. Verse 6 says it was, and verse 8 says the answering did not cancel the accounting.

The word holy appears three times, and Isaiah 6:3 has the same threefold holy in the mouths of the seraphim. The psalm gives no sign of quoting Isaiah, and the resemblance may be no more than a shared liturgical habit, but the pairing has shaped how the psalm is heard. Read with the enthronement psalms that precede it, the sequence moves from a throne above the flood to a throne on the cherubim to a throne with a footstool that human beings are told to touch their heads to, so the mystical reading takes the psalm as a controlled descent rather than a description of height. {{5.4}}, the footstool, is elsewhere in Scripture the ark and the Temple, which puts the lowest point of the divine throne inside a room in Jerusalem. That is the whole geography of the psalm: exalted above all the peoples in verse 2, and reachable at floor level by verse 5.
